newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election - How they vote.
newsitem.headline: French election - How they vote.

text.p: About 39 million French men and women are entitled to vote in Sunday's runoff ballot of a two-stage election to choose a new National Assembly or lower house of parliament.

President Jacques Chirac used his constitutional power to dissolve the Assembly on April 21 and call a snap election 10 months ahead of schedule. The opposition Socialist-Communist-Green bloc scored an upset win in last Sunday's first round.
The president, who appoints the prime minister and cabinet, may not dissolve parliament again in the first year of a new legislature.
Some 6,389 candidates vied for the 577 seats in single-member constituencies in the first round. The record was 29 candidates in a single electoral district in central Paris.
Sunday's runoff is to pick the 565 deputies whose seats were not decided in the first round.

A candidate wins outright if he or she takes more than 50 percent of votes cast on the first ballot. Otherwise, there is a runoff which any candidate who polled 12.5 percent of the total of registered voters has the right to contest.

The person who wins the most votes on the runoff is elected, even if he or she does not poll 50 percent. There are 555 constituencies in metropolitan France and 22 in overseas departments and territories.

In most districts, the ruling conservative RPR-UDF coalition ran a single candidate, whereas the left-wing opposition parties contested the poll separately but united in the runoff behind the best-placed opposition candidate.
Voting in metropolitan France takes place from 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) to 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) in most areas and to 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) in Paris and major provincial cities.

The last overseas departments to vote are in France's Caribbean and South American territories. No results, projections or exit polls may be published until the last polling stations have closed in metropolitan France.
There has been a legal ban on publication of political opinion polls for the past two weeks, since before the final week of the first-round campaign.

On election night, television stations broadcast usually reliable projections of the outcome in votes and forecasts of the result in seats, usually in a spread, as soon as the last nainland voting stations close.
The parties were allotted time for election broadcasts on public radio and television between May 5 and 23. Campaign spending and individual donations to parties are limited by law.
Any party which fields 50 candidates or more receives public funds proportionate to the number of votes it polls.

The centre-right coalition won a landslide majority in the last parliamentary election in March 1993. Then the second-round turnout was 69.2 percent. The state of the parties in the outgoing Assembly was:
RPR (Gaullists) 258
UDF (centre-right) 206
Socialist party and allies 63
Communist party and allies 24
Other left 12
Other right 13
Vacant seat 1
The upper house, the Senate, is elected indirectly by local officials and is not affected by this election.
